av_event.line_text: Idris, he's eight. Just me and him, my mum helps. What do you do for fun, apart from spreadsheets?
av_event.what: A young boy in pyjamas walks across the living room behind Hodan, passing in front of the grey sofa and the folded laundry pile, picks up a book from the shelf and walks back out of frame. Hodan doesn't turn around and keeps talking.

text:
B: Hi! Can you hear me? I'm Hodan, Wembley.
A: Yes, I can hear you. Jibin, I'm near Bristol.
B: Nice. I'm guessing engineer? Your shelves are very organised, I respect that.
A: Thank you. Yes, systems engineer, embedded software, aerospace. And you're NHS? The lanyard.
B: Yeah, senior pharmacy technician. Aseptic unit and dispensary, a hospital in North West London.
A: Okay. My wife is NHS, actually. Ward manager at Southmead.
B: Oh, so she knows. Ward managers, honestly, they're either amazing or they ring down to pharmacy every five minutes asking where their stuff is.
A: She's amazing, obviously. I have to say that.
B: Ha! Obviously. What do you actually do, though, like day to day?
A: Flight-control software verification. Basically proving the code does what it should, every time. Lots of test rigs. If a rig does something strange, they come to me.
B: See, that's the same as me. If something's gone wrong in the department, they come to me. I do the final accuracy checks, I run the rota, and I keep my own spreadsheet of every near-miss, because if you don't track it, it didn't happen, you know.
A: Yes, exactly. Data. People don't like it, but data is data.
B: People hate it. I've got juniors who think I'm scary. I'm not scary, I just don't want anyone getting the wrong drug.
A: To be honest, I have the same reputation. Difficult but usually right.
B: Ha! Difficult but usually right, I'm having that. What band would you be in, if you was NHS?
A: Er, it doesn't map exactly. I'm senior, I want principal. I think I'm overdue, actually. Two people went ahead of me last round and I'm still not sure why.
B: You've got to make noise, though. I pushed through a regrading last year. I just kept going to my manager with evidence until she couldn't say no. Now I want Band 6 lead technician in two years, medicines optimisation.
A: Yes, but sometimes the evidence is there and still. Sorry, what's medicines optimisation exactly?
B: Kind of making sure patients are on the right meds, reviewing, less firefighting. Better hours, better money.
A: Better hours is important. You have a son, I saw the photo?
B: Idris, he's eight. Just me and him, my mum helps. What do you do for fun, apart from spreadsheets?
A: Badminton, Thursdays. Parkrun sometimes, because my GP mentioned my cholesterol.
B: Do you track your times?
A: Of course.
B: Good. I do weights three mornings a week, I log every lift. I did mine at six this morning.
A: Six. Okay, that's dedicated. I struggle with eight on a Saturday.
B: You just get used to it. And badminton, are you competitive?
A: Very. There's one man in our group who never calls his own faults. Every week.
B: Oh my days, I'd be fuming. Sorry, go on.
A: No, it's fine. I argue the line calls. Probably too much, my friends say.
B: Nah, if he's wrong, he's wrong, innit—
